title: Recover a damaged working branch
situation: A feature branch has two accidental commits, a teammate has already pulled it, and you need to back out the change without destroying shared history.

steps.label: Establish the state
steps.reason: Determine whether local edits are uncommitted and whether the commits have been shared.

steps.label: Read the exact patch
steps.reason: Understand which paths and behavior will change before reversing a commit.

steps.label: Revert a shared change
steps.reason: Create a new compensating commit so existing clones and pull-request links remain valid.

steps.label: Validate and publish
steps.reason: Run the project tests before pushing; the revert must remove the faulty behavior without reverting unrelated work.

signals.next: Commit or safely stash the unrelated changes, then retry on a clean tree.
Resolve with intent, test, stage the resolved paths, then continue the revert.

signals.symptom: A secret was exposed in a commit
signals.next: Revoke and rotate it immediately; history editing alone does not make a leaked secret safe.

question.prompt: The bad commit is already on a branch used by other developers. What is generally the safest first fix?
options: Use git revert to create a new correction
question.why: Revert preserves shared ancestry and records a traceable corrective change.

title: Investigate a failing pull-request check
situation: A pull request works on a laptop but fails in CI. The same branch also modifies a GitHub Actions workflow.

steps.label: Read the failed job, not just the badge
steps.reason: Identify whether the failure is a test assertion, missing dependency, denied permission or infrastructure outage.

steps.label: Compare the runner and local environment
steps.reason: Check runtime versions, install flags and environment differences; local caches may hide missing dependencies.

steps.label: Trace changes to the workflow
steps.reason: Treat a workflow edit as code that can alter permissions, execution context and secret handling.

steps.label: Rerun only after addressing the cause
steps.reason: Verify a reproducible install from the lockfile. Require review before elevating workflow token permissions.

signals.symptom: Works locally, fails on clean runner
signals.next: Reproduce on a clean checkout; remove assumptions about local state.
Grant only the precise permission needed to the specific job, not blanket write access.
Separate privileged publishing from untrusted code; use protected environments and review.

question.prompt: A workflow triggered by a pull request needs to publish a release. Which approach best protects credentials?
options: Keep PR tests read-only; publish only from a trusted, approved context
question.why: Untrusted change execution should not inherit credentials capable of changing releases or cloud infrastructure.

title: Find out why a container cannot be reached
situation: The service starts successfully inside a container, but a browser on your host cannot connect to localhost:8080.

steps.label: Confirm the container is running
steps.reason: An exited container is a process failure, not a firewall or DNS issue.

steps.label: Inspect the application log
steps.reason: Look for listen address, runtime exceptions, configuration errors and startup completion.

steps.label: Check the port binding
steps.reason: The host port must be published to the correct container port; EXPOSE alone is metadata.

steps.label: Check the listen address
steps.reason: Inside the container the app normally must bind 0.0.0.0, while the host can publish only to 127.0.0.1 for local use.

signals.next: Correct mapping and service listen address, then recreate the container.

signals.symptom: Works on host but exposed on LAN
signals.next: Restrict host publishing to loopback or an explicit trusted interface.
Use a named volume for durable data, and test backup/restore.

question.prompt: The Dockerfile says EXPOSE 3000. What else is needed to visit the app from the host?
options: Publish the container port and ensure the app listens on the container interface
question.why: EXPOSE documents a port; docker run -p or equivalent Compose ports publishes it.

title: Rescue a broken Compose deployment
situation: A web container starts before its database is ready. Repeated restarts hide the actual error, and a developer suggests adding a ten-second sleep.

steps.label: Validate the Compose model
steps.reason: Resolve variables, service names, volumes and network definitions before launching anything.

steps.label: Inspect service health and exit codes
steps.reason: Distinguish a process crash from an unavailable dependency.

steps.label: Compare service logs
steps.reason: Correlate startup timestamps with authentication, DNS, migration and database readiness errors.

steps.label: Use readiness checks and bounded retries
steps.reason: Provide a meaningful database healthcheck and application reconnect logic instead of a fixed sleep.

signals.inspect: Database health, service name and port
signals.next: Verify DNS and credentials; wait for actual readiness and implement retry/backoff.

signals.symptom: Compose changed but service did not
signals.inspect: docker compose config and image build output
signals.next: Recreate with the intended config and check image tags and bind mounts.
Restore from backup if necessary; avoid down -v when persistent data matters.

question.prompt: Why is depends_on alone often insufficient for a database-backed service?
options: It controls ordering but not full application readiness by default
question.why: Startup order and readiness are different. Healthchecks and application retries close the gap.

title: Diagnose an unavailable Kubernetes service
situation: A Deployment has three replicas, but the Service returns no responses after a rollout.

steps.label: Confirm which cluster is selected
steps.reason: Never start with destructive actions before confirming the target environment.

steps.label: Compare desired and actual state
steps.reason: Spot missing Pods, crash loops, bad rollout status and Service mapping.

steps.label: Inspect readiness and endpoints
steps.command: kubectl get endpointslices && kubectl describe service <name>
steps.reason: Service routing depends on matching labels and ready endpoints.

steps.label: Read events and container logs
steps.reason: Events show scheduling or pull failures; previous logs explain crashes after restarts.

signals.symptom: Service resolves but has no endpoints
signals.next: Correct the selector or readiness probe, not the cluster DNS.
Check capacity, node selectors, taints and volume attachment.
Investigate failing startup, missing configuration and dependency reachability.

question.prompt: The Service exists but its EndpointSlices have no ready endpoints. Where should you look first?
question.why: Without a ready matching backend, the Service cannot forward requests to the intended application.

title: Design a private cloud workload
situation: A small API needs outgoing updates, a private database, backups and limited admin access. A proposed design places everything on the public internet.

steps.label: Draw the trust boundaries
steps.command: Client → public entry point → private application → private database
steps.reason: Separate public user traffic from management planes and backend data paths.

steps.label: Choose least-privilege identity
steps.command: Assign service identity → narrowly scoped permissions
steps.reason: Applications should use short-lived workload identity where available, not long-lived keys in configuration files.

steps.label: Check routes and firewall paths
steps.command: Review inbound, outbound, return path and DNS resolution
steps.reason: Only the intended entry point should be internet-facing; egress can use a controlled gateway where required.

steps.label: Prove the recovery path
steps.command: Back up sample data → restore to isolated environment → verify
steps.reason: A successful backup job is not evidence that a workload meets recovery-time and data-loss targets.

signals.next: Remove public reachability unless explicitly required; isolate the backend in private networking.

signals.inspect: DNS, default route and NAT/egress policy
signals.next: Add only the egress path that is needed, with logging and controls.
Document and time a restore drill against RTO and RPO.

question.prompt: A private VM needs outbound package updates but no direct inbound internet traffic. Which design fits?
options: Controlled outbound routing with tightly restricted inbound rules
Give the VM a public IP and administrator password
question.why: Outbound reachability can be provided without allowing unsolicited inbound connections.

title: Review a risky infrastructure plan
situation: A Terraform plan shows a storage bucket replacement and deletion of an existing security group. The change was intended to update one tag.

steps.label: Confirm workspace and backend
steps.reason: Wrong workspace or state backend can target resources belonging to another environment.

steps.label: Validate the configuration
steps.reason: Catch syntax and schema issues before interpreting the plan.

steps.label: Inspect changes and replacements
steps.reason: Separate intended updates from destructive replacement actions; understand the provider's force-new attributes.

steps.label: Require review and recovery
steps.command: Do not apply until every replacement is explained
steps.reason: For data-bearing resources, verify backup and migration plans. Never treat a plan as routine when it destroys state.

signals.next: Stop and compare desired configuration with current state and drift.

signals.inspect: Whether a legitimate apply is running
signals.next: Coordinate with the state owner; avoid force-unlock without proving the lock is stale.

signals.inspect: Plan drift and untracked manual edits
signals.next: Reconcile deliberately; do not blindly overwrite emergency changes.

question.prompt: An IaC plan unexpectedly replaces a production database. What should happen next?
options: Review the replacement cause and verified recovery plan before any apply
Skip review by applying during low traffic
question.why: Validation checks configuration structure; it does not certify that the planned operational impact is acceptable.

title: Contain a suspicious production release
situation: A new image digest was deployed minutes before an unusual outbound connection and elevated error rate. The incident lead needs a decision that preserves evidence.

steps.label: Establish the timeline
steps.command: Record deploy SHA, image digest, alert timestamps and affected service
steps.reason: Build a shared event sequence before changing systems that may contain useful evidence.

steps.label: Scope the exposure
steps.command: Review identity use, network egress and recent changes
steps.reason: Determine the affected workload, data path and possible credentials at risk.

steps.label: Contain without erasing evidence
steps.command: Isolate suspicious workload or revoke scoped credentials
steps.reason: Use an approved response playbook; capture relevant logs and artifacts first when safe.

steps.label: Restore a verified release
steps.command: Deploy a known-good pinned image digest and check rollback compatibility
steps.reason: Monitor SLOs and compare behavior; rollback does not undo database migrations or data exposure.

signals.inspect: Egress logs, process behavior and build provenance
signals.next: Restrict the suspicious route, preserve telemetry and investigate the artifact.

signals.symptom: Rollback restores service but alerts persist
signals.inspect: Credential reuse and remaining compromised resources
signals.next: Rotate affected credentials and hunt for persistence rather than assuming release rollback resolved compromise.

signals.symptom: Team cannot identify exact image version
signals.inspect: Deployment manifests, registry metadata and CI attestations
signals.next: Require immutable digests and record source-to-artifact relationships for future releases.

question.prompt: What is the strongest evidence that a running container came from an approved build?
options: The deployment and CI records match an immutable signed digest
question.why: A trusted build-to-deployment chain binds an exact artifact digest to reviewed source and provenance.
